blocks.text: By the early 1970s, government survey and engineering offices were routinely using computers for selected calculations: adjusting observations, transforming coordinates, comparing route options and analysing terrain. The paper map remained the normal source and product for much of that work.

blocks.text: The next step was to keep geometry in the machine. Lands and Survey began tracing cadastral features from paper sheets onto digitising tables; computer contouring and photogrammetry brought more measured terrain and imagery into digital form. The output could now be edited, stored and reused as features, not only printed as a table.

blocks.text: For a GIS team, that changed the maintenance job: coordinates still had to be right, but geometry also needed identifiers, continuity and a record of how it had been edited. Chapter 3 follows MAPPAK and the parallel systems that moved New Zealand mapping toward reusable digital features.
